dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe someone who is smart or clever.
examples: That kid is akamai!

dictionary_entries.usage: The ultimate Hawaiian word, representing greetings, farewells, and love.
examples: Aloha, how stay you?

dictionary_entries.usage: The standard local greeting.
examples: Howzit, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe something that is completed.
examples: I pau work.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe a large quantity of something.
examples: Get choke waves today!

dictionary_entries.usage: Expression of gratitude.
examples: Mahalo for the grinds!

dictionary_entries.usage: Reassurance, similar to no problem.
examples: No worry, I got you.

dictionary_entries.usage: Local term for food or eating.
examples: We go get some grindz.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe delicious food.
examples: The poke is real ono!

dictionary_entries.usage: Used for food that is exceptionally delicious.
examples: That kalua pig broke da mouth!

dictionary_entries.usage: Casual address for a male friend or acquaintance.
examples: Eh brah, what's up?

dictionary_entries.usage: Casual address for a female friend.
examples: Howzit, sistah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Term of endearment for a close friend.
examples: Shoots cuz!

dictionary_entries.usage: Formal local spelling of brother/friend.
examples: Eh bruddah, you ready?

dictionary_entries.usage: Verb meaning to be or exist in a state.
examples: I stay hungry.

dictionary_entries.usage: Placed before verbs to indicate past tense.
examples: I wen go beach.

dictionary_entries.usage: Placed before verbs to indicate future tense.
examples: I going surf tomorrow.

dictionary_entries.usage: Indicates inability to do something.
examples: I no can go.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to express desire.
examples: You like go beach?

dictionary_entries.usage: Indicates necessity.
examples: I gotta go home.

dictionary_entries.usage: Indicates past negative action (did not).
examples: I neva go.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describing wild or crazy behavior.
examples: You stay pupule!

dictionary_entries.usage: Local footwear.
examples: Don't forget your slippahs.

dictionary_entries.usage: Term for grandfather.
examples: I go fish with tutu kane.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to the time after work or happy hour.
examples: We go get drinks for pau hana.

dictionary_entries.usage: Expresses agreement or confirmation.
examples: Shoots, see you later!

dictionary_entries.usage: A teacher or guide.
examples: The kumu says to study.

dictionary_entries.usage: Children or child.
examples: The keiki stay playing.

dictionary_entries.usage: Family, including extended family and friends.
examples: We stay ohana.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes something that is a waste or being out of luck / exhausted.
examples: I all poho.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to request a repetition of an action or performance.
examples: Hana hou, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: To eat or get food; also used to describe working hard.
examples: We go grind.
Time for grind.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to childhood days (literally snotty nose days).
examples: Since hanabada days.

dictionary_entries.usage: Means 'later' or 'eventually,' often implying a consequence or result.
examples: Bumbai you learn.
Bumbai we go.

dictionary_entries.usage: Spiritual energy or power.
examples: The place get choke mana.

dictionary_entries.usage: Ghost or supernatural creature.
examples: Spooky obake stories.

dictionary_entries.usage: A visitor or newcomer to the islands.
examples: She one malihini.

dictionary_entries.usage: The land or earth.
examples: Respect the aina.

dictionary_entries.usage: The ocean or sea.
examples: Go makai to the kai.

dictionary_entries.usage: Mountain.
examples: The mauna is covered in snow.

dictionary_entries.usage: Refers to something being entirely finished.
examples: The food is all pau.

dictionary_entries.usage: To be angry or mad.
examples: Don't get huhu.

dictionary_entries.usage: Mischievous or rascal behavior.
examples: That kid is kolohe.

dictionary_entries.usage: Man or male.
examples: He is one kane.

dictionary_entries.usage: An elder or grandparent.
examples: Listen to the kupuna.

dictionary_entries.usage: To do again, or shout for an encore.
examples: Hana hou! Sing one more!

dictionary_entries.usage: To eat or have food.
examples: We go grind.

dictionary_entries.usage: Nasal mucus, commonly used for runny nose in childhood ('hanabada days').
examples: He got hanabada on his face.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used by surfers to describe large, powerful, hollow, or intimidating waves.
examples: Watch out on da outside, da heavies stay rolling in.
Dat north swell brought da heavies today.

dictionary_entries.usage: Being deep inside the hollow curve of a breaking wave or right in the heaviest spot of the impact zone.
examples: He wen drop in right in da pit!
If you stay in da pit, you gotta hold your breath.

dictionary_entries.usage: Poor, blown-out, choppy, or unrideable wave conditions.
examples: Too much wind today, only get junk surf.
No even bother paddle out, stay junk surf.

dictionary_entries.usage: To surf or skate with high performance, throwing heavy carves and turns.
examples: Look at dat grom shred da gnar at Bowls!
We wen shred da gnar all morning.

dictionary_entries.usage: A surf spot where waves peel along a point of land or reef headland.
examples: Dat spot is one classic point break.
Da point break stay firing on dis south swell.

dictionary_entries.usage: Checking the surf or paddling out at the crack of dawn before crowds arrive.
examples: We go dawn patrol tomorrow at 5:30 AM.
Dawn patrol caught da best sets of da day.

dictionary_entries.usage: When a wave crests and breaks entirely at one time across the reef with no open shoulder to ride.
examples: Every wave was one close out, couldn't make da shoulder.
Watch out fo' dat close out on da inside.

dictionary_entries.usage: Major surf etiquette violation where a surfer takes off on a wave in front of someone who already has right of way.
examples: No drop in on da uncles, brah!
He wen drop in on me and lost his board.

dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian-style char siu pork bun, available steamed (traditional white) or baked, sold in local shops and manapua trucks.
examples: Pick up one box of steamed manapua from Chinatown.
Da baked manapua stay piping hot!

english: rice topped with burger, egg and brown gravy
dictionary_entries.usage: Iconic Hawaii comfort dish: a bed of white rice topped with a hamburger patty, fried egg, and rich brown gravy.
examples: Gimme one loco moco with two eggs sunny side up.
After surfing, nothing beat one heavy loco moco.

english: seasoned raw fish bowl over rice
dictionary_entries.usage: Fresh cubed ahi or salmon seasoned with shoyu, sesame oil, and scallions served over warm sushi or white rice.
examples: I going buy one spicy ahi poke bowl fo' lunch.
Dat poke bowl had limu and inamona inside.

dictionary_entries.usage: Having an abundant, delicious spread of local food.
examples: Aunty wen cook choke grindz fo' da graduation party.
Get choke grindz at da potluck, come through!

dictionary_entries.usage: Pidgin slang for food or the act of eating.
examples: Time for kau kau, grab one plate!
You like go kau kau after work?

dictionary_entries.usage: Sweet, sour, and salty dried plum powder used to season gummy candies, fresh fruit (like pineapple and apples), or shave ice.
examples: Sprinkle li hing mui on top da gummy bears.
I like my pineapple with choke li hing mui.

english: grilled spam and rice wrapped in seaweed
dictionary_entries.usage: A staple local Hawaii snack consisting of a block of sushi rice topped with glazed grilled Spam and bound with nori.
examples: Grab two spam musubi from 7-Eleven fo' da beach trip.
Spam musubi is da best pau hana snack.

english: local meat entrée with two scoops rice and macaroni salad
dictionary_entries.usage: The quintessential Hawaii meal consisting of two scoops of white rice, one scoop of macaroni salad, and an entrée meat.
examples: We go drive-in get one chicken katsu plate lunch.
No plate lunch complete without mac salad.

dictionary_entries.usage: A Portuguese yeast doughnut fried until golden, coated in granulated sugar or cinnamon, and optionally filled with haupia or custard.
examples: We stopped at Leonard's Bakery fo' hot malasadas.
Da haupia malasadas stay broke da mouth!

dictionary_entries.usage: Finely shaved ice (not crushed) soaked in tropical flavored syrups, often served over vanilla ice cream with azuki beans and sweetened condensed milk (snow cap).
examples: Hot day like today, time fo' rainbow shave ice with snow cap.
Get da best shave ice on North Shore.

dictionary_entries.usage: Traditional Hawaiian salted, seasoned, and sun-dried beef, often pan-fried before serving.
examples: Dat luau had ono pipikaula and poi.
Pipikaula with hot rice is the best combination.

dictionary_entries.usage: Traditional Hawaiian coconut milk pudding, sliced into blocks or used as dessert pie/cake filling.
examples: Haupia pie is my favorite dessert at Thanksgiving.
Save some haupia for Uncle.

dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian word meaning to slice or cut crosswise into pieces; refers to seasoned diced raw fish (usually yellowfin ahi).
examples: Go buy two pounds shoyu poke for the family.
Fresh caught ahi makes the best poke.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes something physically damaged, a person who is exhausted/beaten up, or people laughing uncontrollably.
examples: His truck was all buss up after the trail.
He told one joke and everybody wen buss up laughing.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes someone who is being fake, disingenuous, or putting on a front.
examples: No act all fakafied, just be yourself.
I can tell when someone stay fakafied.

dictionary_entries.usage: A compliment praising someone for being dependable, true to their word, or doing a great favor.
examples: Thanks for picking me up at the airport, you solid bro.
He always shows up when you need help, solid bro.

dictionary_entries.usage: Exclamation when someone looks extraordinarily fly, does a slick maneuver, or is showing off stylish flair.
examples: Check out his custom rims, too much style!
She caught that wave with too much style.

dictionary_entries.usage: Slang contraction of 'guaranteed'; means something is certain or promised.
examples: Guans we going catch fish today.
You coming tonight? Guans, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Admonition telling someone not to act arrogant, show off in public, or make a fool of themselves.
examples: Just stay cool, no make body in front of everybody.
He started yelling, and his friend said 'no make body, brah.'

dictionary_entries.usage: Giving someone a dirty look or glaring with disapproval or irritation.
examples: Why dat guy giving us stink eye?
My mom gave me stink eye when I didn't take off my shoes.

dictionary_entries.usage: Getting goosebumps from emotional music, spooky ghost stories, or awe-inspiring moments.
examples: Hearing that Hawaiian chant gave me pure chicken skin.
Dat haunted road in Pali gives everybody chicken skin.

english: if it's possible, we'll do it; if not, no worries
dictionary_entries.usage: Philosophical local phrase representing a relaxed, flexible attitude toward life and plans.
examples: You think we can finish today? If can, can; if no can, no can!
Just do your best, if can, can.

dictionary_entries.usage: To speak negatively, gossip maliciously, or badmouth people behind their backs.
examples: No talk stink about your cousins.
She always talking stink about her coworkers.

dictionary_entries.usage: Describes someone who is sulking, grumpy, or throwing a silent tantrum because they didn't get their way.
examples: Why you stay all habut? It was just a game.
He got habut and walked home by himself.

english: go for a leisure drive or stroll
dictionary_entries.usage: To go out exploring, driving, strolling, or visiting friends with no strict agenda.
examples: Sunday morning we go holoholo on the East Side.
Uncle went holoholo down to the harbor.

dictionary_entries.usage: Enthusiastic contraction of 'all right' used to express agreement, celebration, or excitement.
examples: Aurite! We going beach!
You got the job? Aurite!

english: go for it with full energy
dictionary_entries.usage: Encouragement telling someone to go hard, give full effort, or strike with intensity.
examples: Gee vum, brah! You can score the touchdown!
Time to study for finals, gee vum!

english: getting completely defeated in a game
dictionary_entries.usage: Can refer to a short buzz haircut, or figuratively to being soundly defeated without scoring a point.
examples: He got one fresh shave head for summer.
We got shave head in volleyball today, 21-0.

dictionary_entries.usage: Local pronunciation of 'roger that' meaning affirmative, acknowledged, or agreed.
examples: Meet at 6 PM? Rajah dat!
Rajah dat, I'll bring the cooler.

dictionary_entries.usage: An outdoor porch, covered patio, or open-air veranda on a home or condo.
examples: Let's sit out on the lanai and drink coffee.
The apartment has a huge lanai with ocean views.

dictionary_entries.usage: Cardinal direction in Hawaii meaning toward the mountains or inland (opposite of makai).
examples: Turn mauka at the next intersection.
The mauka side of the highway is clear.

dictionary_entries.usage: Cardinal direction in Hawaii meaning toward the ocean or sea (opposite of mauka).
examples: The park is on the makai side of the street.
Walk makai until you reach the shoreline.

english: local rice dish with hamburger patty, egg, and gravy
dictionary_entries.usage: A staple Hawaii diner comfort dish composed of a bowl of hot white rice topped with a hamburger patty, a sunny-side-up fried egg, and rich brown gravy.
examples: Ho, I stay starving, we go get one loco moco from da diner.
Two scoop rice and extra gravy on top da loco moco.

english: salted salmon side dish with tomatoes and onions
dictionary_entries.usage: A classic Hawaiian side dish made with diced salted salmon, ripe crushed tomatoes, sweet Maui onions, and crushed ice.
examples: No forget da lomi salmon for da luau plate.
Lomi salmon taste so ono wit poi and kalua pork.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian (lomi = massage or mix by hand)

english: octopus or squid simmered in taro leaves and coconut milk
dictionary_entries.usage: A cherished traditional Hawaiian stew prepared by slow-cooking tender octopus or squid with young luau (taro) leaves, coconut milk, and sea salt.
examples: My tutu make da best squid luau on da island.
Squid luau stay rich and sweet from da coconut milk.

dictionary_entries.usage: A chewy, sweet, glutinous rice cake that is a beloved dessert across Hawaii, appearing in variations like butter mochi, chi chi dango, and strawberry mochi.
examples: Aunty brought fresh butter mochi to da potluck.
Dis strawberry mochi stay broke da mouth.

dictionary_entries.usage: A friendly local slang term for a mixed-breed dog, or affectionately for someone of mixed heritage / multicultural background.
examples: My dog is one rescue poi dog, smart as anything.
He got one loyal poi dog dat follow him everywhere.

dictionary_entries.usage: A large platter of mixed appetizers and finger foods served at parties, pau hana gatherings, and local diners.
examples: Order da pupu platter while we wait for da main food.
Da pupu platter get lumpia, chicken wings, and edamame.

dictionary_entries.usage: The essential Pidgin comparative meaning 'much better', 'superior', or 'way more enjoyable'.
examples: Going early morning is mo bettah, no get traffic.
Homemade poke stay mo bettah than store-bought.

dictionary_entries.usage: A common loan phrase used in Hawaii conversation to tell someone to pause, slow down, or wait a second.
examples: Chotto matte brah, I still tying my shoes.
Chotto matte, lemme check da directions first.

english: Puerto Rican dance music in Hawaii
dictionary_entries.usage: A lively genre of Puerto Rican dance music created by immigrants to Hawaii plantations, characterized by accordion, cuatro, and guiro rhythm.
examples: Dey playing kachi kachi music at da graduation party!
Everyone was dancing to da kachi kachi band.
dictionary_entries.origin: Puerto Rican plantation culture in Hawaii

dictionary_entries.usage: Originally sugarcane fiber waste; colloquially used in local plantation slang as a playful or biting term for a rascal or good-for-nothing.
examples: Dat guy acting like real bagasu.
Clean up all dat bagasu from da yard.

dictionary_entries.usage: A button on clothing, or a button on an electronic switch/device.
examples: Push da botan for open da gate.
Your shirt missing one botan, brah.

dictionary_entries.usage: Plantation-era slang word for breaking wind or flatulence.
examples: Who wen make totus in da car?!
Crack da window, someone wen make totus.

english: do not make a fool of yourself
dictionary_entries.usage: Admonition instructing someone to behave with common sense and stop acting crazy or stupid.
examples: Behave in front da kumu, no make lolo.
No make lolo on camera, brah!

dictionary_entries.usage: Severe highway or island road congestion where cars are packed tightly bumper-to-bumper.
examples: H-1 get choke traffic right now, take da back road.
We was late because had choke traffic going town-bound.

dictionary_entries.usage: A traditional beach necklace or jewelry item made from the worn, naturally holed tip of cone shells found along Hawaiian shorelines.
examples: He wearing his vintage puka shell necklace.
We went hunting for puka shells along da shoreline.

english: island greeting accompanied by shaka sign
dictionary_entries.usage: The quintessential friendly Hawaii greeting and hand gesture expressing goodwill, friendliness, and solidarity.
examples: Shaka brah, good for see you!
Threw him one big shaka brah when he let us merge.

dictionary_entries.usage: Heart, feelings, affection, or moral character. Commonly used in Hawaiian and local expressions of sincerity, aloha, and heartfelt emotion.
examples: From da bottom of my puʻuwai, mahalo nui loa.
Uncle get one big puʻuwai, always taking care da family.
Listen to your puʻuwai when you need for choose da right path.

dictionary_entries.usage: As an adjective, stink describes a bad attitude, not a bad smell: someone acting stink is being mean or rude. It also shows up in stink face (a scowl), alongside stink eye and talk stink.
examples: How come you acting so stink to me?
No be stink, share da musubi wit your sistah.
He get one stink attitude today, no talk to him.
dictionary_entries.origin: From English 'stink', extended in Pidgin from a bad smell to a bad attitude.

english: pork slow-cooked in an underground oven
dictionary_entries.usage: A whole pig cooked in an imu (underground oven) until smoky and tender, then shredded; a lūʻau staple. At home and in plate lunches it is usually made in an oven or slow cooker with Hawaiian salt. Also called kalua pork.
examples: Get kalua pig and cabbage at da plate lunch place.
Uncle wen dig da imu fo' da kalua pig.
Fo' da baby lūʻau get kalua pig, lomi salmon, and poi.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian kālua, to bake in an imu (underground oven).

dictionary_entries.usage: A Pidgin way to say thanks a lot: Hawaiian mahalo plus English plenty (a lot). More casual than mahalo nui loa.
examples: Mahalo plenty fo' da ride, cuz!
Aunty, mahalo plenty fo' da food.
Mahalo plenty, brah, you saved me.

dictionary_entries.usage: Pidgin pronunciation of 'better': the final -er becomes -ah, as in braddah and sistah. At the start of a sentence it means 'you had better' (Bettah you go now). Best known in mo' bettah.
examples: Bettah you go now before da traffic.
Dis one bettah, try taste.
You feeling bettah today?

dictionary_entries.usage: Teasing description of thick, sturdy legs, likened to a daikon radish. Playful between friends, but it is a jab about someone's body, so know your audience.
examples: Ho, dat soccer player get daikon legs, strong!
She wen tease me 'cause I get daikon legs.
All da hiking wen give me daikon legs.
dictionary_entries.origin: From Japanese daikon-ashi (radish legs), brought by Japanese immigrants to Hawaii.

dictionary_entries.usage: Famous island phrase and motto celebrating Maui island pride: 'Maui is the best' or 'Maui is top of the line'. Frequently seen on island bumper stickers, shirts, and signs.
examples: No matta where you go, Maui no ka oi, brah.
Ho, dat sunset from Haleakala proves Maui no ka oi.
Chee-hoo! Maui no ka oi all day!

dictionary_entries.usage: Island Pidgin expression meaning to keep something confidential, secret, or discreet ('on the down-low'). Used when telling someone not to broadcast sensitive news or gossip.
examples: Keep dis news on da lo lo yo, no tell nobody yet.
We stay planning one surprise party, so stay on da lo lo yo.
Brah, dat deal went down on da lo lo yo.
dictionary_entries.origin: Blend of English 'on the down-low' / 'low-low' with Pidgin rhythm and rhyming marker 'yo'.

dictionary_entries.usage: Traditional and formal Hawaiian letter or email sign-off meaning 'with gratitude' or 'with thanks'. Commonly seen as a closing valediction in local correspondence, formal messages, and community announcements.
examples: Me ka mahalo for your kokua and support.
He wen sign da letter 'Me ka mahalo, Uncle Kimo.'
Me ka mahalo nui loa to all our volunteers today.

dictionary_entries.usage: A Hawaii Chinese-local dim sum classic (siu mai) featuring seasoned ground pork, water chestnuts, and shrimp steamed in an open wonton wrapper.
examples: Grab two manapua and tree pork hash from da bakery.
Dip da pork hash in hot mustard and shoyu, so ono!
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaii Chinese-plantation culinary adaptation of Cantonese siu mai (烧卖).

dictionary_entries.usage: The classic Hawaii local milestone question and phrase describing graduating from school, especially high school, which serves as a core local connection in Hawaii.
examples: What year you went grad?
We wen grad together from McKinley.
His keiki wen grad college on da mainland.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian Pidgin past-tense preverbal marker 'wen/went' + English 'grad' (graduate).

dictionary_entries.usage: A traditional calming beverage prepared from the roots of the kava plant (Piper methysticum), shared across the Pacific and Hawaii during ceremonies and community gatherings.
examples: Come join da kava circle tonight and talk story.
Drinking kava helps you relax and pau hana in peace.

dictionary_entries.usage: The ancient Hawaiian harvest festival and new year season dedicated to Lono, god of agriculture and fertility, marked by games, sports, feasts, and peace.
examples: During Makahiki season, warfare was forbidden across da islands.
Hauʻoli Makahiki Hou means Happy New Year!

dictionary_entries.usage: The legendary watermen and surf instructors of Waikiki who helped popularize surfing worldwide while serving as ambassadors of aloha.
examples: Uncle was one Waikiki beach boy from small kid time.
Da beach boys know how fo read every single wave.

dictionary_entries.usage: An elegant, formal, floor-length Hawaiian gown with a train, adapted in the 19th century from missionary dresses into a dignified symbol of Hawaiian royalty and modern formal attire.
examples: Tutu wore her velvet holokū for da May Day pageant.
Da singer looked stunning in her silk holokū.

dictionary_entries.usage: Everyday colloquial phrase indicating immediate agreement and that no further explanation or convincing is necessary.
examples: Free food and live music? Nuff said, I stay dea!
Nuff said brah, pack your gear and we go.

dictionary_entries.usage: A casual Pidgin farewell and parting expression meaning 'alright then' or 'see you then'.
examples: Shoots, I see you tomorrow, jah den!
Jah den brah, take care!
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian Pidgin contraction of 'just then' or 'alright then'.

dictionary_entries.usage: Plantation-era island exclamation expressing disbelief, shock, surprise, or distress.
examples: Ay koodish! How come da tyre stay flat?
Ay koodish, look at da long line!

dictionary_entries.usage: Local slang describing someone with wide, bulging, tired, or blankly staring eyes, resembling an aku (skipjack tuna). Similar to menpachi eyes.
examples: Why you got aku eye like dat? You nevah sleep last night?
He stayed looking at da waves wit aku eye.

dictionary_entries.usage: Local Pidgin term referring to a Catholic priest, pastor, or clerical father figure.
examples: Fadah man wen give da blessing befo' we eat.
Uncle went talk story wit da fadah man aftah church.

dictionary_entries.usage: Casual island hand greeting incorporating a slap, slide, or fist bump between friends and braddahs.
examples: Give da boy dap when you see him.
Shoots brah, throw me one dap.
dictionary_entries.origin: Colloquial greeting gesture adopted widely in island culture.

dictionary_entries.usage: Hawaiian Pidgin phonetic pronunciation and spelling of special. Widely recognized in Hawaii literature and everyday speech.
examples: Dis one stay real spesho to me.
Da Good An Spesho Book stay da Pidgin Old Testament.
dictionary_entries.origin: Hawaiian Pidgin phonetic pronunciation of English special.

dictionary_entries.usage: Everyday Pidgin term for vomiting or throwing up. Follows the standard Pidgin th-stopping ("th" -> "t").
examples: Too much malasada, now I feel like I going trow up.
Dat boat ride was rough, almost everyone wen trow up.
dictionary_entries.origin: Pidgin phonology for English throw up.

dictionary_entries.usage: A Samoan term widely embraced across Hawaii meaning brother or close friend, used similarly to brah or bro.
examples: Cheee, what's up uso!
Dat guy my uso from way back, we grew up together.
dictionary_entries.origin: Samoan uso (sibling of the same gender). Commonly used in local Hawaii culture.

dictionary_entries.usage: Used to describe someone who acts entitled, fussy, or demanding like a spoiled child. Commonly heard as "spoil brat".
examples: No be so spoil, eat what stay on your plate.
Dat kid stay one spoil brat when he no get his way.
dictionary_entries.origin: English spoiled, adapted with characteristic Pidgin consonant cluster reduction.

stories.title: First Day on the Job
stories.pidgin_text: Ho brah, my first day work was one trip! Da boss tell me, 'Eh, you da new guy yeah? No worry, we going show you how we do.' I was so nervous, hands stay shaking. But den dis one aunty from accounting come ovah, 'Eh, relax. We all ohana hea. You like some coffee?' She wen bring me one fresh malasada too. By pau hana time, I felt like I been working dea my whole life. Dat's da aloha spirit, brah.
stories.english_translation: Wow man, my first day of work was quite an experience! The boss tells me, 'Hey, you're the new guy right? Don't worry, we're going to show you how we do things.' I was so nervous, my hands were shaking. But then this one lady from accounting came over, 'Hey, relax. We're all family here. Would you like some coffee?' She brought me a fresh malasada too. By the end of work, I felt like I had been working there my whole life. That's the aloha spirit, man.
stories.cultural_notes: Hawaiian workplaces often have a strong sense of 'ohana' (family). Malasadas are Portuguese donuts that are extremely popular in Hawaii. 'Pau hana' refers to the time after work is finished.

stories.title: Fishing with Grandpa
stories.pidgin_text: Every Saturday, me and my tutu kane go down da pier fo' fish. He get his special spot, been going dea since small kid time. 'Eh, you gotta be patient,' he always tell me. 'Da fish going come when dey ready.' We sit dea, talk story about da old days. He tell me about when Haleiwa was all pineapple fields. No cars, no tourists, just da locals. 'Ho, was different time,' he say, looking at da ocean. I love dose days with tutu. Dat's how we pass down da culture, one fishing trip at a time.
stories.english_translation: Every Saturday, my grandfather and I go down to the pier to fish. He has his special spot, been going there since he was a child. 'Hey, you've got to be patient,' he always tells me. 'The fish will come when they're ready.' We sit there, chatting about the old days. He tells me about when Haleiwa was all pineapple fields. No cars, no tourists, just the locals. 'Wow, it was a different time,' he says, looking at the ocean. I love those days with grandpa. That's how we pass down the culture, one fishing trip at a time.
stories.cultural_notes: Fishing is an important cultural activity in Hawaii, passed down through generations. 'Tutu kane' is the Hawaiian term for grandfather.
